rewrites.summary:
Kebbi runs Sharia criminal law as one of the twelve northern states that had adopted it by 2002, with Sharia courts exercising criminal jurisdiction over Muslim defendants in parallel with the federal system (Human Rights Watch, 2004). The federal penal code criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide, and the UK Home Office country note (June 2025) records that these twelve states' Sharia penal codes extend that criminalisation to same-sex acts between women, with a maximum of death for men and flogging or imprisonment for women.

No Kebbi-specific enforcement record against trans people exists; the case-level documentation of Sharia enforcement covers three other bloc states (USCIRF study, 2017). For a Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor who is outed, the practical difference from the rest of the country is jurisdictional: exposure to a Sharia court applying a criminal code that is broader in scope and harsher in penalty than the federal statute alone.
rewrites.blindSummary: This state is among twelve in the country's north that operate an enacted religious criminal jurisdiction over the Muslim population (parallel courts with criminal competence), documented by a major rights watch in 2004. A 2025 government country note records that these states' religious penal codes criminalise same-sex conduct more broadly than the federal statute and reach acts between women, with death a maximum for men and flogging or imprisonment for women. No state-specific enforcement record against trans people exists; the case documentation of this system covers three other states in the bloc. For a visitor, the difference from the federal baseline is jurisdictional: a religious court's criminal code, broader and harsher, applied to Muslims and perceived Muslims.

Government religious-freedom commission study of this bloc's religious criminal-law implementation (173 cases, 2017; PDF not retrievable at fetch time) covers three other states; this state is not separately documented.

rewrites.summary:
Niger State operates Sharia criminal law as part of the twelve-state northern bloc adopted by 2002, with Sharia courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslim defendants (Human Rights Watch, 2004). The federal anti-discrimination statute criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide; the UK Home Office country note (June 2025) records that the Sharia layer in these states extends criminalisation to acts between women.

No Kebbi-style state-specific enforcement or Hisbah record against trans people is documented for Niger; case-level enforcement records exist for other bloc states. The Sharia system adds a parallel criminal jurisdiction that the federation's southern states do not have, under which an outed Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor faces broader charges and harsher penalties than under federal law alone.
rewrites.blindSummary: A state within a twelve-state northern bloc operating an enacted religious criminal jurisdiction over Muslim defendants since 2002 (rights-watch documentation), parallel to the federal statute that criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide; a 2025 government note confirms the religious codes extend that criminalisation to acts between women. No state-level enforcement record against trans people exists; the enforcement record covers other bloc states. The risk for an outed Muslim or perceived-Muslim visitor is the parallel jurisdiction itself: broader scope, harsher penalties than the federal baseline.

Government country policy note (June 2025) on sexual-orientation and gender-identity law (cached front-matter only; content catalogued in the research dossier): documents the hybrid system, the twelve-state religious criminal layer and its coverage of women, and limits in arrest data.

rewrites.summary:
Imo combines community violence with active state policing against gay people. In April 2018 a crowd in Isiala Mbano stripped two men accused of gay sex, beat them and paraded them through the streets with palm leaves tied around them; a follow-up report records that police took the two men in custody. In February 2025 the state police command announced it had stormed a 'same-sex party' at a hotel in Owerri, arresting eight suspects and charging them under the 2014 anti-homosexuality law, citing its 14-year term — the command's briefing expressly framed the enforcement as covering a 'gay, lesbian, bisexual and/or transgender act'.

The pattern runs across years and across modalities: mob justice met without accountability in 2018, and named, state-command enforcement invoking the criminal law in 2025. For a discovered visitor here, risk comes from neighbours and police alike.
rewrites.blindSummary: A state where documented action against gay people has come from both a crowd and the police: in April 2018 a mob stripped, beat and paraded two men accused of gay sex through the streets of one of its towns, with a follow-up report recording their seizure by police; in February 2025 the state police command announced it had raided a same-sex gathering at a hotel in the state capital, arresting eight people and charging them under the national anti-homosexuality law, citing the 14-year penalty, with the command's briefing naming bisexual and transgender acts among its targets. Both the informal and the formal pathway are documented, seven years apart.
blindSourceSummaries: Activist monitoring report (April 2018): two men in a town of this state were stripped, beaten and paraded by a crowd accusing them of gay sex, then taken by police per a follow-up; the outlet situates the attack in rising mob justice enabled by the national anti-gay law.

National news report (February 2025): the state police command announced storming a same-sex party at a hotel in the state capital, arresting eight suspects charged under the anti-homosexuality law (14-year term cited), the briefing expressly naming bisexual and transgender acts.
rewrites.notes: Score/deviation clause deleted; both incidents retained on their cited reports; dates and charges preserved.

rewrites.summary:
In May 2018 in Ekpoma, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. The coverage framed the act as an 'abominable' one defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land', and no prosecution is recorded: customary moral judgement operating lethally, with complete impunity. For national context, a rights-monitoring report published in January 2025 documented 556 violations against real or perceived LGBT people affecting 850 victims across Nigeria in 2024 — and states these are only a fraction of the true scale.

Edo's finding is the Ekpoma killing itself: where a discovered visitor can face lethal 'community justice' invoked in the name of tradition, answered afterwards by nobody.
rewrites.blindSummary: In May 2018 in a town of this state, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and one escaped, the coverage framing the act as 'abominable' and against 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land', with no prosecution recorded. A national rights-group report (January 2025) counted 556 violations against real or perceived LGBT people in this country in 2024 affecting 850 victims, and describes that count as a fraction of the true scale. The state's documented pathway is lethal community violence in the name of custom, followed by total impunity.
blindSourceSummaries: National news report (May 2018): two men discovered by their community in a town of this state; one lynched, one escaped; framed as an 'abominable act' against traditional laws and heritage; no prosecution recorded (cache captured navigation only; incident detail catalogued in the research dossier).

Equal-rights initiative annual report (published January 2025): 556 violations against people on the basis of real or perceived SOGIESC in this country in 2024, affecting 850 victims, described as a fraction of true scale.
rewrites.notes: 'Belt' generalisation dropped to the incident; score line deleted; national monitoring kept as context.

rewrites.summary:
Aceh is the only province in this country operating a codified religious criminal law of its own: the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014) criminalises same-sex conduct (liwath, musahaqah) and close proximity (khalwat), with public caning as its signature punishment, applied by Islamic Shariah courts and policed by the Wilayatul Hisbah religious force alongside the secular Satpol PP units. Enforcement is active and widening: in August 2025 a Sharia court — sitting behind closed doors — sentenced two men to 80 strokes each for hugging and kissing, caned in a public park before around 100 spectators, with eight more people caned the same day; up to 100 strokes are available for morality offences generally, and Amnesty International called the practice 'state-sanctioned discrimination and cruelty'.

The Qanun does not name transgender people, but enforcement reaches them: a February 2025 boarding-house round-up detained a waria and a gay student facing up to 100 strokes under the liwath provision, with officials urging landlords to police tenants; in January 2018 police detained twelve transwomen and shaved their heads to teach them 'how to act like real men'. Private consensual conduct that carries no criminal penalty in any other province here can be publicly caned by a court in Aceh.
rewrites.blindSummary: The only province in this country operating its own codified religious criminal law under special autonomy: same-sex conduct and close-proximity offences carry public caning (up to 100 strokes for morality offences broadly), sentenced by religious courts and policed by a religious vice force with civil-enforcement support. The recent record shows widening application: in August 2025 a closed-door religious-court conviction for hugging and kissing led to 80 strokes each for two young men, caned in a park before crowds, with eight more caned the same day; in February 2025 a boarding-house round-up detained a transfeminine person and a male student facing up to 100 strokes under the same-sex-conduct provision; in January 2018 police detained twelve transfeminine people and shaved their heads. Private consensual conduct legal in every other province is canable here; an international rights body has called the practice state-sanctioned cruelty.
blindSourceSummaries: Law-and-culture journal study (2025): how this province's special religious criminal code (same-sex conduct and proximity offences) is enforced, including caning sentences, against visible gender nonconformity, with recurring boarding-house monitoring.

Wire-service report (August 2025): two men publicly caned 80 strokes each in the provincial capital for hugging and kissing after a closed-door religious-court conviction, before ~100 spectators; eight more caned the same day; the province permits up to 100 strokes for morality offences; a rights group called it state-sanctioned discrimination and cruelty.

Local reporting (February 2025): civil defence and religious police detained a transfeminine person and a gay student in a boarding-house, facing up to 100 caning strokes under the same-sex-conduct provision; enforcement officials urged lodging-keepers to report tenants.

University human-rights institute commentary: transgender women are the most frequent victims of this country's anti-LGBT enforcement upturn; records the January 2018 detention and forced head-shaving of twelve transwomen by this province's police.
rewrites.notes: Score/deviation and West Java lines deleted; unsupported 159-stroke caning dropped; only claim-backed facts kept.

rewrites.summary:
KwaZulu-Natal is where documented street violence against queer people meets the country's most powerful traditional authority. A 2024 criminology study from a university in the province documents queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in KwaMashu, a township north of Durban — daily life in which the constitutional guarantee of equality does not reach. In January 2012 the Zulu King's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival made the collision explicit: the royal house insisted the reported 'rotten' wording was a mistranslation; the South African Human Rights Commission said it would investigate; the provincial premier backed the royal family; and the Congress of Traditional Leaders of South Africa (CONTRALESA) responded that the Pietermaritzburg gay and lesbian network demanding an apology had shown the king 'disrespect' and was 'only seeking fame'.

For a discovered visitor, the province's pattern is that local moral authority — monarchy, chiefly councils, and the provincial government siding with them — has publicly ranged against queer claims, while academic documentation shows queerphobic violence persisting in its townships.
rewrites.blindSummary: A province containing the country's largest traditional monarchy, where a 2024 university criminology study documents queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer minorities in a township north of the province's main city, despite constitutional equality guarantees. In January 2012, anti-gay remarks by the leading traditional monarch at a harvest ceremony produced a striking alignment: the national human-rights commission opened an investigation, the provincial premier backed the royal house (which claimed mistranslation), and the national assembly of traditional leaders condemned the gay and lesbian network that sought an apology as 'disrespectful' and 'only seeking fame'. Documented township violence coexists with traditional and provincial authority ranged against queer claims.
blindSourceSummaries: University criminology master's thesis from this province (2024): queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in a township north of the province's main city, situated within the country's endemic crime and hate-crime context despite constitutional equality guarantees.

LGBT news report (January 2012): after anti-gay harvest-festival remarks by an influential traditional monarch, the royal house claimed mistranslation, the national human-rights commission opened an investigation, the provincial premier backed the monarchy, and the national congress of traditional leaders called the gay network demanding an apology disrespectful and fame-seeking.
rewrites.notes: Bantustan/Mogale and no-statute clauses dropped (no claims); study and king facts kept; score deleted.

rewrites.summary:
Mpumalanga is where the country's official house of traditional leaders launched its organised campaign against constitutional equality for queer people. Meeting at Hazyview in June 2010, the National House of Traditional Leaders and its provincial houses — while professing to 'respect' the Constitutional Court's same-sex marriage judgment — resolved that 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts', declared their opposition to legal recognition, warned of ostracism and violence, and vowed a five-year campaign against it. Reporting in 2016 documented the same body asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause that protects people from discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

This is official traditional-structure hostility, taken on this province's soil and stated as durable climate rather than enacted law: there is no provincial statute against queer people, no enforcement against visitors, and no retrieved Mpumalanga-specific trans-incident series. The finding is the platform the country's chiefhood announced here — and did not retract.
rewrites.blindSummary: A town in this province hosted, in June 2010, the national assembly of traditional leaders' formal launch of a five-year campaign against legal recognition of same-sex relationships — 'respecting' the top court's marriage judgment in words while resolving that traditional leaders are 'disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts' and warning of ostracism and violence; by 2016 the same body was reported as asking parliament to review the constitution's sexual-orientation equality clause. The province's finding is institutional climate, not enacted law: no provincial statute, no enforcement against visitors, and no local incident series are documented.
blindSourceSummaries: Published letter (June 2010) of the national and provincial houses of traditional leaders after a meeting in a town of this province: rejecting legal recognition of same-sex unions, 'disappointed' the courts had given the practice 'a lifeline', warning of ostracism and violence, vowing a five-year campaign.

Radio report (July 2016; page not retrievable at fetch time, content catalogued in the research dossier): the same national traditional-leaders body asked parliament to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination based on sexual orientation.
rewrites.notes: Daily-Maverick, Bantustan and PEPUDA clauses dropped (no claims); meeting facts kept; score deleted.

rewrites.summary:
Limpopo's rural life runs through chiefs and traditional courts to a degree that makes the parallel customary-law system the province's defining risk factor. Human Rights Watch's analysis of the legislation at issue warned that it 'establishes a separate legal system for people living in the former Bantustans' and 'threatens to undermine this security for millions of South Africans living in rural areas', 'particularly for the exercise of gender and sexual rights' — because chiefs and traditional courts adjudicate personal-status and morality-adjacent matters under customary law, with a consent presumption running against the individual. The later record, from a 2025 verification pass: the bill was enacted as the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act of 2019, and was then declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court in 2023, with the declaration suspended and the Act's validity extended while Parliament works on a replacement. A 2012 activist report — 'culture of the chiefs threatens our rights' — pressed the same case contemporaneously.

No statute criminalises a visitor's expression here and no trans-specific incident series is recorded. But for an outed visitor in rural Limpopo, the practical moral authority is often the chief's court rather than the ordinary court — and that jurisdiction's record on gender and sexuality runs against the individual. The absence of recorded incidents reflects under-reporting, not demonstrated safety.
rewrites.blindSummary: Much of this province is rural former-homeland ground where chiefs and their courts adjudicate personal-status and morality questions under customary law. A rights group's legal analysis (2012; page unretrievable at fetch time, content catalogued in the research dossier) warned the resulting legislation 'establishes a separate legal system' for these areas and threatens gender and sexual rights, with a consent presumption running against the individual; a 2025 verification records that the law was enacted in 2019, then declared unconstitutional in 2023, its validity suspended for a parliamentary replacement window. No statute criminalises queer expression and no incident series is documented; the risk to an outed visitor is jurisdictional — the local authority most likely to judge them is a chief's court, whose customary record runs against the individual — and silence in the data means under-reporting, not safety.
blindSourceSummaries: Rights group legal analysis (May 2012; page not retrievable at fetch time, content catalogued in the research dossier): the traditional-courts bill, later enacted in 2019, establishes a separate legal system in the former homelands and threatens gender and sexual rights, because chiefs' courts decide morality and personal-status matters under customary law with a consent presumption against the individual.

Community-media report (April 2012; site gone): chiefs' courts adjudicating personal-status and morality matters under customary law threaten gender and sexual rights in former-homeland rural areas — the same core claim as the contemporaneous legal analysis.
rewrites.notes: Density superlative dropped (unsourced); Mogale kept via freshness; score/sibling lines deleted.

rewrites.summary:
Gauteng — the province containing Johannesburg and Pretoria — is where the country's protections are most visibly operational. It hosts the first representative quantitative study of hate crimes against gay and lesbian people ever conducted anywhere in this country (2003/04, by an LGBT well-being institute with a university applied-psychology centre, documenting prevalence, consequences and contributing factors, with the era's leading community organisations as partners). A 2016 national campaign review confirms only three such studies exist in the country's history, placing Gauteng squarely in the small tier of provinces where the evidence, reporting channels and NGO capacity demonstrably exist. There is no province-specific ban or enforcement action here: the national constitution enumerates sexual orientation, and the equality statute and hate-crime framework operate uniformly, with the courts, prosecutors and civil society that apply them most concentrated in this province.

One caveat cuts both ways: the province's comparatively high recorded hate-crime volume — the very reason the evidence exists — may partly reflect better reporting infrastructure rather than greater danger. The operational conclusion stands either way: an incident a visitor reports here is likeliest to meet a functioning institutional response.
rewrites.blindSummary: The province containing this country's largest city and its administrative seat hosts the country's first representative quantitative provincial study of hate crimes against gay and lesbian people (2003/04, an LGBT well-being institute with a university research centre and a coalition of community organisations); a 2016 national review counts only three such studies ever conducted here, putting this province in the small tier where evidence, reporting channels and NGO capacity are demonstrably present. There is no province-level ban or enforcement; the national constitution, equality law and hate-crime framework operate uniformly, and the courts, prosecutors and civil society that apply them are most concentrated here. Recorded-volume may partly reflect better reporting — but an incident reported in this province is likeliest to meet a functioning institutional response.
blindSourceSummaries: Research report (2003/04): the country's first representative quantitative provincial study of hate crimes against gay and lesbian people, in this province — prevalence, consequences and contributing factors — by an LGBT well-being institute with a university applied-psychology centre and a partner roster of the era's leading community organisations.

National campaign research review (2016, hosted by an LGBT archive): only three quantitative studies of anti-LGBT hate crime exist in this country — a 2003 multi-province survey including this province, a 2010 study of another province, and this campaign study; measures national levels of discrimination.
rewrites.notes: HSRC/paradox and PEPUDA-detail clauses dropped (no claims); superlatives recast onto the two studies; score deleted.

rewrites.summary:
Chechnya's security apparatus operates outside legal constraint on this question. In February 2017, law-enforcement and security officials launched an anti-gay purge: dozens of men were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities, starved and tortured; some were forcibly disappeared; others were returned to their families 'barely alive from beatings' after their captors exposed them to relatives encouraged to carry out honour killings (Human Rights Watch, 2017). Independent domestic reporting in January 2019 found the persecution resuming and the documented secret facility active again, while the regional leader's press office denied such sites exist. Since 2022, two investigations have documented detained homosexual men blackmailed into 'volunteering' for front-line conscription in Russia's war in Ukraine (at least seven sent, one killed) and a mass wave of unlawful detentions tied to forced mobilisation. The UK Home Office note (June 2025) records systematic campaigns in this republic and the wider North Caucasus from 2017 to 2024 — abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings — and assesses trans people and visible advocates as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with such violence spreading beyond the region after the 2023 'extremist movement' designation.

For a discovered or outed visitor: detention without legal process, torture, coerced conscription or death, with no functioning judicial remedy.

Independent domestic reporting in January 2019 recorded resumed persecution and renewed activity at a documented secret facility, against official denials that such sites exist. From 2022, two investigations document detained gay men blackmailed into front-line conscription for a foreign war (at least seven sent, one killed) and a mass wave of unlawful detentions tied to forced mobilisation. A 2025 government country note finds a systematic 2017–2024 campaign of abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings here, rating trans people and visible advocates as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with the 2023 'extremist movement' designation extending enforcement beyond this region. For an outed visitor: detention outside the law, torture, conscription or death; no functioning judicial remedy.
